extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, early-stage CEOs, and startup PR/marketing people
extracted.subtask_description: How to craft and pitch a one-page press release and accompanying email to generate media coverage for a startup announcement (launches, funding, acquisitions, etc.). Includes strategy on exclusives/embargoes and post-publication amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal of PR / own a space
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of PR is to own a space — to colonise an industry and make you or your company the go-to for comment and direction. The immediate aim is to generate press coverage that leads to ongoing mentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think beyond a single story: use PR to build long-term mind-share (e.g., how Dave McClure owns 'accelerators' and 'investments'). Use guest articles and press releases together to build authority and ensure future coverage even without new announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — 'What is your story?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Your announcement must be 'new' and genuinely newsworthy; journalists look for interesting, timely stories, not yesterday's news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical eye-catching announcements include company and product launches, takeovers (the more aggressive/expensive the better), and funding announcements — but anything can be newsworthy with the right timing. Work out clearly what announcement you are making and why it matters now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release length and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be about a page long and they must not leave factual holes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it concise (≈1 page) while providing all essential facts so journalists don't have gaps to chase. If you aren't confident in writing, have a grammar/attention-to-detail friend proofread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline / title format
rubrics_metrics.description: A headline for your release, essentially in the format of: 'Something/someone does/experiences/announces something new'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a clear, newsy headline that summarizes the announcement. Make it informative and focused on the new action or development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (first) paragraph — date, location, mission
rubrics_metrics.description: First Paragraph: Discuss the larger mission of the new announcement, i.e. what it does and what it is for. Include a date and location at the very beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put date and location up-front (standard press-release convention) and immediately explain the core purpose/mission of the announcement so reporters understand the 'what' and 'why' quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second paragraph — specifics of the product/announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Second paragraph: Delve into the specifics of your product / announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the concrete details (features, terms, participants, numbers) a reporter would need to explain the announcement accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an initial CEO/co‑founder quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Third paragraph: A quote from your CEO or a business co-founder explaining the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least one ready-to-use quote so journalists don't have to source one; use the quote to convey significance, vision, or human context. This saves time for reporters and increases the chance of accurate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize with industry trends and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth paragraph: Bring in trends to explain why this announcement is relevant to the larger industry / community that your business is a part of. Ideally this will include at least one data point (ex: how large the industry is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a supporting data point or trend to demonstrate relevance and provide reporters with a broader angle. This helps frame the story beyond a company-centric announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final quote to wrap up
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth paragraph: Wrap up with a final quote from your CEO or founder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a closing quote to reinforce the key message or future outlook; it provides an editorial hook and additional usable copy for articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company background and media contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth paragraph: Briefly sum up the history of your company and the background of its leader(s). Also include a contact for journalists to use if they want more in-depth information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a short boilerplate/company history and clear contact details (name, email, phone) so reporters can follow up for interviews or clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the email pitch personal — the email sells the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The press release does not sell a journalist on covering the story, the email does. Pitching the press release will happen by email. Make your email a bit more personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research the specific journalist (use the correct name), reference recent relevant work, and personalize the pitch to their beat. A mistaken name or a generic pitch reduces pickup chances. Use example templates as starting points but tailor each message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research journalists and avoid basic mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the journalist in question’s name and make sure you don’t use the wrong one. Remember, you only have one shot at a first impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check spellings, beats, and recent coverage. Target reporters who are likely to care, rather than sending blind blasts; a well-targeted email improves pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define a coverage strategy: blanket vs exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you want blanket coverage (sending to many journalists with an embargo) or offer an exclusive to one outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using blanket, coordinate with an embargo and ask journalists to respect it. Embargo norms vary by region (UK journalists often accept EMBARGO on a release; in the US you should ask first). Consider offering an exclusive to control timing and maximize pickup in a top publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using embargoes effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: If you opt for blanket coverage, entrepreneurs coordinate that coverage by asking journalists to respect an embargo. Put 'EMBARGO' above your release or ask the journalist to agree to an embargo first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know regional norms (UK vs US) and always confirm embargo terms with journalists. An embargo is not a guarantee — it relies on journalist agreement — so plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer exclusives strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering the announcement as an exclusive gives a specific publication the right to publish first and can increase the chance of coverage, especially from larger outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: larger publications may take exclusives more seriously; exclusives can lead to pickup by other outlets; a big niche publication can open doors to mainstream coverage. Be prepared to offer interviews or founder time to other outlets afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplify coverage after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the article comes online, share it across social media, send it to investors/customers/employees, and email other publications with the link (carefully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask your network to share; have the journalist notify you when the piece is live; offering founder time to other outlets can help convert interest. Avoid rubbing competitors' noses in the exclusive — be diplomatic when approaching others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a media cadence — repeat announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases help establish a media cycle. Ideally repeat every 8–12 weeks, or whenever you have a substantive announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat PR as ongoing work: evaluate what worked, plan the next announcement, and keep building visibility rather than expecting one-time virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guest articles alongside press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest articles (by a business leader or ghostwritten) are an effective complement to press releases for building authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guest pieces to position leaders as industry authorities and drive long-term thought leadership; combine with releases to own topical space.
